archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose quarterback-driven passing game can beat anyone, paired with a defense that only has to be average and opportunistic to carry the rest.

report.headline: Burrow's passing game is elite, and an average defense is finally enough.
report.take:
This is Joe Burrow's offense, and the coaches know it. Cincinnati passes more than any team in the league relative to game situation (pass rate over expected 10.6, first), and that aggression is earned: the dropback game is second in EPA per play at 0.269 and second in success rate. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins soak up the targets, Chase Brown is a real third option out of the backfield, and the run game exists mostly to keep defenses honest. At 30.9 points a game, the offense has turned a 7-2 record into something closer to inevitable than lucky.

The real story is on the other side of the ball, though, because the Bengals have had good offenses before. In 2024 the offense ranked 7th in EPA and the team went 9-8 behind a defense that ranked 27th. Last year the defense fell to 29th and the team went 6-11. This year it sits 16th in EPA allowed, which is unremarkable on its face but is the difference between wasting Burrow and riding him. That middling defense gets there with a pressure rate that ranks 6th, 13 takeaways (5th), and a red zone that tightens up (42.9% touchdowns allowed, 5th).

The numbers flatter the defense in places. It ranks 30th on third down, 27th in rush EPA allowed and 26th in yards allowed per game, so it gives up drives and then relies on the red zone and turnovers to limit the damage. Those two are the noisiest parts of any defensive profile. The record is mostly clean: wins over expected is a modest 0.92, the point differential implies about six wins, and the one-score record is ordinary. The early games were won by defense while the passing offense sputtered (negative pass EPA in Weeks 1 and 2). Since the losses to Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, the offense has carried everything.

Where it goes from here depends on two things: protection and how much the defense gives back. Burrow holds the ball longer than almost anyone (2.665 seconds, 29th) behind a line that ranks 23rd in pressure allowed. Guard Dalton Risner's knee and two tackles working back from injury make that a live question. If the line holds, this offense is good enough to win the North and push for a top seed. The defense doesn't need to get better, only to avoid sliding back toward last year.

strengths.title: Elite, aggressive dropback passing
strengths.body: Cincinnati passes more than any team relative to situation and gets the second-best EPA per dropback in the league. It runs through Burrow and a deep receiver room led by Chase and Higgins. A starting quarterback this efficient over nine games, with no change at the position, is about as stable as football production gets. Week 10's 21.4 passing EPA against Pittsburgh shows it is still climbing.

strengths.title: Pressure and takeaways cover the gaps
strengths.body: The front gets home at the league's 6th-best rate, and the defense has turned that into 13 takeaways (5th). Several games swung on it, including four takeaways against Tampa Bay in the opener. Pressure tends to hold up from week to week. Takeaways usually come down somewhat, and edge Cashius Howell's stint on IR thins the rotation.

strengths.title: Red-zone defense limits the damage
strengths.body: Opponents move the ball, but only 42.9% of their red-zone trips end in touchdowns, 5th in the league. That is why a defense 26th in yards allowed sits mid-pack in points. It is real value so far, but red-zone rates on nine games of trips are among the least stable numbers in the sport.

concerns.title: Defense can't get off the field
concerns.body: Opponents convert 47.5% of third downs, 30th in the league, and the run defense is 27th in EPA allowed with explosive runs a recurring leak. This is a real flaw rather than a cost of style, and it is how Pittsburgh won in Week 3 with 138 rushing yards. If the red-zone stops regress, these sustained drives turn into points.

concerns.title: Protection is thinning
concerns.body: Burrow keeps the sack rate low (8th) by getting the ball out under duress, but the line ranks 23rd in pressure allowed, and he has one of the longest times to throw in the league. Risner, a 94%-snap guard, left the Pittsburgh game with a knee injury. Myles Hinton and Brian Parker II are working back at tackle, so depth is a problem. If the interior is a backup, that pressure rate will start to show up as sacks.

concerns.title: Run game is a spectator
concerns.body: Backs get just 2.18 yards before contact (26th), and rushing EPA was negative in most games. Against Jacksonville that left a 23-yard rushing day and a loss in which Burrow threw for 428 yards. It mostly reflects a pass-first identity, but it means the offense has no fallback when the passing game is off or protection breaks.

trend.note: After a slow passing start and back-to-back losses to Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, Cincinnati hasn't lost since early October. Passing EPA has been in double digits every game since Week 5, peaking at 21.4 in the Pittsburgh rematch.

nextGame.headline: Chase and the tight end draw Washington's softest coverage spots
nextGame.body:
The Bengals go to Washington as 6.5-point favorites (-290) with a 52.5 total, and the matchup points at Burrow. Washington's pass defense ranks 22nd in EPA per play and 27th in sack rate, so Burrow should have time. The Commanders have been hurt most by opposing WR1s (29th) and TE1s (32nd), which is exactly where Chase and Mike Gesicki line up. They also allow touchdowns on 75% of red-zone trips (29th), so Cincinnati's drives should finish. Washington's offense is 21st in EPA with Jayden Daniels starting every game but one. Its backs get more yards before contact than any team's, but the run game still ranks 20th in EPA, which tests Cincinnati's soft run defense without being built to punish it.

Availability matters most on Cincinnati's line. Risner's knee, Hinton's illness and Parker's IR return all bear on who protects Burrow. With Andrei Iosivas out, Dohnte Meyers keeps the WR3 snaps. Corner Jalen Davis has been designated to return, while safety Kyle Dugger is out and Howell remains on IR. Washington is missing guard Lucas Patrick, tackle Laremy Tunsil (out into December) and lead back Jacory Croskey-Merritt, whose practice window hasn't opened. That is a thin offense to ask to keep pace in a shootout.

waysToWin.title: Feed Chase against Washington's soft spot
waysToWin.body: Washington has let opposing WR1s run well above their usual output, and Chase leads the team in targets by a wide margin. Its weak pass rush gives Burrow the time he likes to hold the ball. That matchup alone can push Cincinnati past 30.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Washington's defense gives up touchdowns on most red-zone trips and has been the league's worst against tight ends. Gesicki and Brown near the goal line turn drives into sevens. That builds the margin that forces Washington away from its run game.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a patched Washington line
waysToWin.body: Without Patrick and Tunsil, Washington's line, already 23rd in pressure allowed, faces a front that pressures at the 6th-best rate. Pressure forcing Daniels into quick decisions is how Cincinnati's defense has manufactured takeaways all year.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways feed Washington's ball-hawks
waysToLose.body: Washington is 3rd in turnover differential per game, and Cincinnati's offense has given the ball away in bunches before, with four turnovers in the Tennessee shootout. Short fields would let a middling Washington offense hang around in a high-total game.

waysToLose.title: Third downs extend Washington drives
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati's defense is 30th on third down and soft against the run. Washington's backs get to the second level clean. Long drives shorten the game and keep Burrow on the sideline, which is how Pittsburgh won the first meeting.

waysToLose.title: Short game smothered, line breaks
waysToLose.body: Washington defends short passes well (8th) and rarely allows explosive runs (3rd). If Risner can't go and the interior struggles, Burrow's long-developing throws could become the hits and sacks the line has mostly avoided so far.

nextGame.watch: Whether Risner's knee lets him play, and how well Burrow's protection holds on longer-developing throws if it doesn't.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable part. A top-three passing attack with the same quarterback all season, a high-volume receiver duo and a pass-first plan that fits it won't fade without an injury. The schedule is kind for most of the stretch: New Orleans, Carolina, Indianapolis and Baltimore all rank outside the top 12 on both sides of the ball. The real tests are Kansas City and two games against a Cleveland defense ranked 9th, with the division at stake.

The defense is where to expect some give. Its red-zone and takeaway numbers are carrying a unit that allows long drives, and the history says Cincinnati defenses haven't held a mid-pack ranking lately. Expect points allowed to drift up a little and the margins to tighten. The offense still makes them a strong bet to win the North and contend for a bye.
swingFactors: Offensive line health with Risner and the tackles
Whether red-zone defense and takeaways hold up
The two Cleveland games and Kansas City

confidence.note: Nine games, one quarterback, and efficiency that matches the record; the defense is the volatile part.
